draft.title: Budj Bim and land management
card: Budj Bim is in western Victoria, on the Country of the Gunditjmara people. Long ago a volcano erupted there and left lava flows and wetlands.
The Gunditjmara built channels and weirs across the lava flows. A weir is a low wall that holds back or guides water. These works trapped eels and let people farm them, thousands of years ago.
The eels gave the Gunditjmara a steady supply of food. The system shows that people managed the land and water with planning and skill, and it was built over many generations.

Elsewhere in Australia, First Nations peoples used cultural burning and water management to care for Country. Cultural burning is the use of small, controlled fires set for a purpose, guided by knowledge of the land.
draft.remember: First Nations peoples shaped and cared for Country, as the Gunditjmara did with eel channels and weirs at Budj Bim.

a.q: What did the Gunditjmara build at Budj Bim, and why?
opts: Channels and weirs, to trap and farm eels
Channels and weirs, to protect the land from rising seas
Stone walls, to keep out megafauna such as Diprotodon
Grindstones, to grind seeds into flour for food
a.why: The Gunditjmara built channels and weirs to hold and guide water so they could trap and farm eels. Grindstones were used for seeds and are a different kind of technology, not the eel system.
a.clue: Think about the food that came from the wetlands.

b.q: A guide at Budj Bim tells Year 7 students that the Gunditjmara managed their land and water. Which fact best supports what the guide says?
opts: They built channels and weirs that trapped and farmed eels
They lived in western Victoria for many years
They moved around the lava flows to find wild eels
They told stories about the volcano that erupted there
b.why: Building channels and weirs shows planned work that changed how water moved, which is management of land and water. Living in a place, moving about or telling stories does not by itself show that the land and water were managed.
b.clue: Which answer shows something people built and planned?

a.best: Channels and weirs, to trap and farm eels

b.best: They built channels and weirs that trapped and farmed eels

problems.detail: The clue 'Which answer shows something people built and planned?' gives the answer away. Only one option mentions building anything, so a student can pick it without understanding what land and water management means.

check.summary: The facts on the card and in both questions check out. However, question b's clue points straight to the only option about building, so it gives the answer away and should be reworded.

proposal.title: Budj Bim and land management
card: Budj Bim is in western Victoria, on the Country of the Gunditjmara people. Long ago a volcano erupted there and left lava flows and wetlands.
The Gunditjmara built channels and weirs across the lava flows. A weir is a low wall that holds back or guides water. These works trapped eels and let people farm them, thousands of years ago.

The eels gave the Gunditjmara a steady supply of food. Managing land and water means changing how it works with planning and skill, not just using what nature gives. The Budj Bim system was built over many generations.

Elsewhere in Australia, First Nations peoples used cultural burning and water management to care for Country. Cultural burning is the use of small, controlled fires set for a purpose, guided by knowledge of the land.
proposal.remember: First Nations peoples shaped and cared for Country, as the Gunditjmara did with eel channels and weirs at Budj Bim.

a.q: What did the Gunditjmara build at Budj Bim, and why?
opts: Channels and weirs, to trap and farm eels
Channels and weirs, to protect the land from rising seas
Stone walls, to keep out megafauna such as Diprotodon
Grindstones, to grind seeds into flour for food
a.why: The Gunditjmara built channels and weirs to hold and guide water so they could trap and farm eels. Protection from rising seas sounds close because it also involves water, but the works were built for eels.
a.clue: Think about the food that came from the wetlands.

b.q: A guide at Budj Bim tells Year 7 students that the Gunditjmara managed water there. Which fact best supports what the guide says?
opts: They built weirs that guided water into eel traps
They caught eels that swam freely in natural creeks
They camped beside the wetlands to be close to food
They told stories about the volcano that erupted there
b.why: Building weirs changed how the water moved, with planning, so that eels could be trapped and farmed. That is water management. Catching eels in natural creeks is tempting because it involves eels and water, but it only uses what nature gives and does not change the water.
b.clue: Managing means more than using what nature provides.
